rationale: Tests the ASOM/myringotomy quadrant known-trap: students frequently confuse anteroinferior with posteroinferior. Block 3 covers ASOM clinical presentation which sets up the surgical anatomy context.
Block 9 covers principles of management and myringotomy, testing understanding of the stage-guided approach and indications for myringotomy versus antibiotics.
Block 6 covers examination and investigations in OME. Tympanometry type B with normal canal volume is the hallmark finding; students confuse type B with type C.
Block 9 covers management of OME. The clinical pearl at block 10 highlights that adult OME requires flexible nasendoscopy to exclude nasopharyngeal carcinoma — a critical safety trap.
Block 4 covers safe vs unsafe distinction in CSOM. This is the defining CSOM known-trap: mucosal/tubotympanic type is the SAFE type with a central perforation in the pars tensa.
Block 9 covers management including myringotomy and tympanoplasty. Tests application of surgical indications and the underlay graft principle.
Block 4 covers cholesteatoma anatomy and pathophysiology. The CSOM safe/unsafe known-trap: squamosal CSOM is the unsafe type with attic/marginal perforation and cholesteatoma.
Block 9 covers surgical management and types of mastoidectomy. Tests the student's ability to distinguish canal wall up from canal wall down procedures and their indications.
Block 4 covers anatomy of spread. Tests understanding of the routes by which CSOM infection reaches extracranial and intracranial sites — critical for explaining why cholesteatoma is dangerous.

Block 9 covers management of CSOM complications. The clinical pearl at block 10 notes that 'sudden drying of the ear' in active CSOM may signal an intracranial complication — a dangerous diagnostic trap.
Block 4 covers anatomy and physiology of the Eustachian tube. Tests understanding of the muscle responsible for active ET opening — a frequently tested anatomical fact.
Block 9 covers management of ET disorders. The clinical pearl at block 10 highlights that inserting a grommet for patulous ET (autophony) will worsen symptoms — a critical management trap.
